diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose that a finite index set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{N}^{d}$ is downward-closed in one direction.

we say that an index set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{N}^{d}$ is \textit{downward-closed in one direction} if there is a coordinate index $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ such that whenever $(1,\dots1,\ell,1\dots,1)\in\Lambda$ holds, where $\ell$ is in the $j$-th position, then for all integers $k\leq\ell$ we also have $(1,\dots1,k,1\dots,1)\in\Lambda$.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated hypothesis is only an implication, so a finite $\Lambda$ satisfying it vacuously in every direction may have an empty first-coordinate axis slice (e.g. $\Lambda=\{(1,3)\}$ in $d=2$). For such sets the asserted existence of $\overline{\ell}_{1}$ with $(\ell_1,1,\dots,1)\in\Lambda$ for all $\ell_1\le\overline{\ell}_1$ is false, so the fooling-function reduction $S_{\Lambda}(h_{\Lambda})=Q_{\overline{\ell}_1}^{\mathrm{uni}}(p_n)$ cannot be performed as written. The conclusion itself survives: if the axis slice is empty then $S_{\Lambda}(h_{\Lambda})=0$ directly and the same one-dimensional estimate with $n=n_1\le N$ applies.

failure_location.quote: Without loss of generality, we assume that $\Lambda$ is downward-closed in the first coordinate. Then, for some $\overline{\ell}_{1}\in\mathbb{N}$ we have $(\ell_{1},1\dots,1)\in\Lambda$ for all $\ell_{1}=1,\dots,\overline{\ell}_{1}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the degenerate case: if $\Lambda$ contains no point of the form $(\ell,1,\dots,1)$, take $h_{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol x)=p_{n_1}(x_1)$; then every summand vanishes since $\Delta_{\ell}(1)=0$ for $\ell\ne1$, so $S_{\Lambda}(h_{\Lambda})=0$ and the same univariate lower bound gives the claim.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem thm:GH-lower-bound-general (and, by repetition, of Theorem thm:added-1) does not cover all index sets allowed by the hypothesis; the stated rates remain true after a trivial case split.
issues.title: Lower-bound proof assumes an axis point that the hypothesis does not guarantee
issues.why_classification: A short local case split re-establishes the identical conclusion; no rate, constant, or advertised claim is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where $\mathscr{I}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{uni}}$ is the polynomial interpolation operator using the zeros of $H_{n_{\ell}+1}$.
let $\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n}$ be the roots of the univariate Hermite polynomial $H_{n}$ of degree $n$.

issues.failure_explanation: The fooling function $p_n$ is built from the $n=n_{\overline{\ell}_1}$ Gauss--Hermite nodes (zeros of $H_n$), while the sparse-grid interpolation $\mathscr{I}_{\Lambda}$ is built from interpolation operators using the $n+1$ zeros of $H_{n+1}$. Since $\int \mathscr{I}_{\overline{\ell}_1}^{\mathrm{uni}}(p_n)\,\rho\,\mathrm{d}x$ is the interpolatory quadrature at the interpolation nodes, where $p_n$ does not vanish, the displayed equality (identifying the GH-rule error with the integral of the interpolation error) is false, and the reduction to the known univariate lower bound collapses. Rebuilding $h_{\Lambda}$ from the zeros of $H_{n_{\overline{\ell}_1}+1}$ repairs the argument, and $n_{\overline{\ell}_1}+1\le N$ preserves both stated bounds.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define the fooling function from the zeros of $H_{n_{\overline{\ell}_1}+1}$ (the actual interpolation nodes), so that $\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{uni}}_{\overline{\ell}_1}(p)=0$, and keep the remaining bookkeeping ($N\ge n_{\overline{\ell}_1}+1$); the cited univariate analysis applies verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem thm:added-1 (general and isotropic lower bounds for sparse-grid Gauss--Hermite interpolation) does not establish the stated rates; the statements themselves are true once the fooling function is built from the interpolation nodes.
issues.title: Interpolation lower bound pairs the fooling function with the wrong univariate rule
issues.why_classification: A contained, routine correction of the fooling-function construction (one level shift) restores the proof with no change to the stated rates.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The value $b$ controls the truncation error, namely the integral of $f\rho$ over $\mathbb{R}^d\setminus [-\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{b}]$, whereas $Q_N$ controls the numerical integration error.
First, we will show that $f\in H_{\rho}^{\alpha}$ implies $\|f\rho\|_{\text{unanchored}}+\|f\rho\|_{\text{decay}}\leq C_{d,\alpha}\|f\|_{H_{\rho}^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}$

issues.failure_explanation: The rule \eqref{eq:affine-QMC} only approximates the integral over $[-\boldsymbol b,\boldsymbol b]^d$, while the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:aff-lattice-error} contains the full Gaussian integral, so the truncation tail must be bounded; the proof never does so, and at the stated $b=\sqrt{\alpha\ln N/2}$ it cannot be. Indeed, for $f_b(\boldsymbol x)=\psi(x_1-(b+1))$ with fixed $\psi\in C_c^{\infty}$, $\|f_b\|_{H^\alpha_\rho}\le C_\alpha$ uniformly in $b$, while $Q_N(f_b)=0$ and $|I(f_b)|\ge c\,\bar\Phi(b+3/4)\asymp \mathrm{e}^{-b^2/2}/\sqrt{\ln N}=N^{-\alpha/4-o(1)}$. Thus the worst-case error is $\Omega(N^{-\alpha/4-o(1)})$, which exceeds $C_{\alpha,d}N^{-\alpha}(\ln N)^{\frac{3\alpha d}{2}+\frac d4}$ for all large $N$: the proposition is false as stated.

failure_location.quote:
let $Q_{N}$ be the rank-$1$ lattice rule
defined in \eqref{eq:affine-QMC} with $b=\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2}\ln N}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Enlarge the truncation, e.g. take $b=2\sqrt{\alpha\ln N}$ exactly as in Proposition prop:added-2, so the tail is $\bar\Phi(b)\asymp N^{-2\alpha}$ and is absorbed; the embedding argument in the proof is scale-independent, and the lattice part is then re-verified at the new scale.
issues.overall_effect: The affine-lattice case of Proposition prop:lattice-affin and the corresponding row of Theorem thm:qmc-summary (and the prose claiming rate-optimality of this construction) are unreliable: with $b=\sqrt{\alpha\ln N/2}$ the truncation error alone decays only like $N^{-\alpha/4}$.
issues.title: Affinely-mapped lattice proposition ignores the domain-truncation error
issues.why_classification: The repair is a contained reoptimization of one parameter (the truncation constant, mirroring the parallel digital-net result), after which the same proof architecture delivers a recognizably comparable, rate-optimal bound; no advertised regime or guarantee type is lost, but the specific stated bound cannot be kept.

issues.failure_explanation: For $r\ge1$ and $1\le\eta\le r$ the quantities $C_{r,\eta}(t)=B_{r,\eta}(\Phi'(t),\ldots,\Phi^{(r-\eta+1)}(t))$ and their derivatives appearing in the identity require derivatives of $\Phi$ up to order $r+1$; under the stated hypothesis (mere differentiability) these objects, and hence the claimed identity, are undefined, so the lemma is ill-posed as stated and its proof cannot start. In the only application ($\Phi=\phi\in C^{\infty}$) the strengthened hypothesis holds, so nothing downstream is lost.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the hypothesis to $\Phi\in C^{r+1}((0,1))$ (or $C^{\infty}$); the given proof then applies verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma lem:Bell-recursive-uni is inapplicable/ill-defined for general differentiable $\Phi$ as claimed; with the strengthened hypothesis all its uses (the component-wise Faà di Bruno formula) remain valid.
issues.title: Bell-polynomial lemma assumes only differentiability though its objects need higher derivatives
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard smoothness hypothesis repairs the lemma locally; the conclusion and every application (which use a smooth $\Phi$) are preserved.
